entities.summary:
Pacificus of Ceredano, born Pacificus Ramati around 1420 in the Lombardy region of Italy, emerged as a significant figure within the late medieval Franciscan Observant reform movement, a period marked by renewed asceticism and spiritual rigor within the Catholic Church. His life, culminating in his death on June 13, 1482, in Milan, exemplifies the fervent religious devotion and intellectual currents of 15th-century Italy, primarily through his dedicated preaching and contributions to Franciscan spirituality. His eventual beatification by Pope Benedict XIV in 1745 cemented his enduring legacy as a venerated member of the Order of Friars Minor, influencing subsequent generations of religious life and hagiographical tradition.

A tireless itinerant preacher, Pacificus traversed much of northern Italy, delivering sermons that resonated deeply with both monastic communities and the laity. He was a central figure in the Observant reform, advocating for a stricter adherence to the Rule of Saint Francis, particularly concerning poverty and communal living, a stance that often placed him in dialogue with, and occasionally opposition to, more conventual factions within the Franciscan Order. Beyond his powerful oratory, Pacificus also authored significant theological works, including the 'Summa Pacifica,' a comprehensive treatise on moral theology and canon law that became a standard text for Franciscan confessors and scholars for centuries after his death.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Pacificus of Ceredano's 'Summa Pacifica' served as a foundational text for Franciscan moral theology, influencing confessional practices and spiritual guidance for centuries. His beatification solidified his position as a venerated figure, perpetuating the ideals of the Franciscan Observant reform.
